title: Introduction to Linguistics
tagline: Language and linguistics, the nature of language, phonetics and phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, language and society, language change, and the languages of the world and of China
summary: Linguistics studies human language in general, and seeing Chinese as one language among thousands changes how a native speaker understands it. This course introduces the nature of language and the core fields of linguistics — phonetics and phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and pragmatics — with examples from Chinese and other languages, and then turns to language in society, how languages change, and the languages of the world and of China.
overview: This course is the toolbox. Earlier courses taught you to notice that a Chinese sentence is awkward, that a rhyme has shifted, that a character was misread; here we name the machinery that makes those judgements possible: the level of analysis (sound, form, sentence, meaning, use), and what each level is entitled to explain.

We move through the five core components in the standard order - phonetics and phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics - but each chapter is anchored in Chinese data, because Chinese is not a neutral illustration of textbook categories: it stresses them. Wordhood, tense, plurality, constituency and even the sentence itself all behave differently here, and that difference is the point.

Then we widen to the two dimensions that no grammar can hold: society (register, style, region, identity, prestige, language policy) and time (sound change, reanalysis, grammaticalisation, lexical turnover). A language is not a system that happens to change; it is a record of changes that have not yet been smoothed over.

Finally the course places the scientific study of Chinese in its own history: from philology and the Qieyun tradition to the Mashi Wentong, the Yuya Xuncode, the twentieth-century reconstruction of Old and Middle Chinese and the post-1980 reform of Chinese grammar - so that you can tell which of your intuitions about Chinese are linguistic facts and which are curriculum habits.
outcomes: Distinguish levels of analysis and state, for a given datum, which level can settle the question and which is being smuggled in.
Transcribe, describe and classify the sounds of Chinese with working IPA competence, and separate phonetic substance from phonological opposition.
Give a defensible test for wordhood and for constituency in Chinese, and explain why morphological criteria borrowed from Indo-European languages fail here.
Compare major syntactic frameworks on a fixed set of Chinese constructions (ba, bei, topic-comment, classifiers, shi...de) without pretending the frameworks are equivalent.
Analyse lexical and compositional meaning using sense relations, componential features and referential tools, and know their limits on figurative language.
Explain speech acts, implicature, deixis, politeness and discourse structure with Chinese examples, and identify which apparent semantic puzzle is in fact pragmatic.
Handle the sociolinguistic and diachronic vocabulary - variety, register, prestige, standardisation, reanalysis, grammaticalisation, lexical diffusion - well enough to read primary research.
Situate the study of Chinese historically and describe the languages of China non-politically, including the difference between script affiliation and genetic affiliation.

chapters.title: Language and linguistics
chapters.summary: What linguistics studies, description and prescription, and the history of the discipline from traditional philology to Saussure and Chomsky.

chapters.title: The nature of language
chapters.summary: Language as a system of signs, arbitrariness and linearity, language and thought, and human language compared with animal communication.

chapters.title: Phonetics and phonology
chapters.summary: The International Phonetic Alphabet, phonemes and allophones, distinctive features, and syllables and tones in the languages of the world.

chapters.title: Morphology
chapters.summary: Morphemes and words, inflection and derivation, and isolating, agglutinative and fusional languages.

chapters.title: Syntax
chapters.summary: Constituents and hierarchy, the typology of word order, and the main approaches to syntax.

chapters.title: Semantics
chapters.summary: Lexical meaning, componential analysis, sentence meaning, presupposition and entailment.

chapters.title: Pragmatics
chapters.summary: Deixis, speech acts, the cooperative principle and politeness.

chapters.title: Language and society
chapters.summary: Varieties, standard languages, bilingualism, language contact, and language policy in China.

chapters.title: Language change
chapters.summary: Sound change, grammaticalisation and lexical change, and the comparative method.

chapters.title: Languages of the world and of China
chapters.summary: Language families and typology, and the languages spoken in China and the families they are usually assigned to: Sino-Tibetan, Altaic, Austroasiatic, Austronesian, Indo-European and others.

history.title: A grammar for Chinese appears
history.detail: Ma Jianzhong's Mashi Wentong applies a Latin-derived part-of-speech frame to classical Chinese: the beginning of Chinese grammar as a discipline, and of a century-long argument about fit.

history.title: Course in General Linguistics
history.detail: Published posthumously from student notes; sign, arbitrariness, langue and parole, synchrony and diachrony become the default vocabulary of linguistics.

history.title: The Qieyun rhyme handbook
history.detail: A character lookup arranged by reading; for the next millennium, phonology in China meant commenting on this one book.

history.title: A Grammar of the National Language
history.detail: Li Jinxi's grammar of vernacular Chinese supplies the subject-predicate-and-adjunct vocabulary still used in schools.

history.title: The Institute of History and Philology and its Bulletin
history.detail: Modern research on Chinese historical phonology and dialects is institutionalised alongside the vernacular movement.
history.people: Luo Changpei, Li Fanggui, Zhao Yuanren

history.title: Étude sur l'ancienne phonétique chinoise
history.detail: Karlgren brings the comparative method to the rhyme tables and reconstructions of old and middle Chinese follow.

history.title: Language
history.detail: Bloomfield's distributional method sets the standard for two decades of American work, and trains a generation of Chinese linguists.

history.title: Principles of Phonology
history.detail: The Prague School account of the phoneme, opposition and markedness gives phonology its structural apparatus.

history.title: Syntactic Structures
history.detail: Grammar is redefined as a generative device rather than a catalogue of inspected sentences, reshaping syntax and, within a decade, work on Chinese.

history.title: Essential Grammar of Chinese and the pinyin scheme
history.detail: Lu Shuxiang's grammar organises Chinese around constructions and semantic roles; that year the state promulgates Hanyu Pinyin.
history.people: Lu Shuxiang; the Writing Reform Committee

history.title: How to Do Things with Words
history.detail: Austin's lectures publish the doctrine that saying is doing; pragmatics begins as a discipline with a name.

history.title: Logic and Conversation
history.detail: Grice's implicature supplies a general model of how speakers mean more than they say and how hearers work it out.

history.title: Lectures on Chinese Grammar
history.detail: Zhu Dexi reformulates subject, predicate, phrase and construction using distributional tests drawn from Chinese itself.

references.title: Mashi Wentong (《马氏文通》)
references.note: The first systematic grammar of classical Chinese.

references.title: Course in General Linguistics
references.note: Sign, value, synchrony: the founding text of structuralism.

references.title: An Essay on the Phonology of the Chinese Languages
references.note: Chinese historical phonology argued with both the rhyme tradition and the comparative method.

references.title: Essential Grammar of Chinese (《中国文法要略》)
references.note: Construction and meaning in Chinese, written as a comparative grammar.

references.title: Syntactic Structures
references.note: Grammar as a generative device, not a catalogue.

references.title: Spoken Chinese (《汉语口语》)
references.note: Descriptions of living spoken Chinese by its finest analyst.

references.title: Lectures on Chinese Grammar (《语法讲义》)
references.note: Distributional tests applied to Chinese, in Chinese.

references.title: Elements of General Linguistics
references.authors: H. Hock (or: Xu Degong, Introduction to Linguistics)
references.note: The standard Chinese textbook through which most readers meet the discipline.
